Redis is essentially a very fast

. Unlike traditional databases such as PostgreSQL or MySQL, which primarily store data on disk, Redis keeps most of its data in RAM. Because RAM access is extremely fast, Redis can serve requests with very low latency, often in microseconds or a few milliseconds. That speed is the main reason Redis became so widely adopted in backend systems.
At first glance Redis looks like a

. You save a value under some key and later retrieve it. But Redis became popular because it evolved far beyond a basic dictionary. It supports multiple specialized data structures such as lists, sets, hashes, sorted sets, streams, and more. These structures allow developers to model many common backend problems directly inside Redis without building complex logic themselves.
The most common use of Redis is

. Imagine a web application that constantly requests the same information from a slower database. If every user request hits the database directly, the database becomes overloaded and response times increase. Redis sits in front of the database and stores recently or frequently requested data in memory. Instead of performing an expensive database query every time, the application can retrieve the value from Redis almost instantly. In many systems Redis dramatically reduces database load and makes applications feel much more responsive.

. When users log into a website, the server often needs temporary information associated with their session, such as authentication state, permissions, or shopping cart contents. Redis works extremely well here because it supports automatic expiration of data. You can tell Redis to delete an entry after a certain amount of time, which is perfect for sessions, temporary tokens, verification codes, or short-lived caches.
Redis is also commonly used as a

. Modern applications frequently offload expensive work into background jobs instead of processing everything immediately during a user request. For example, image resizing, video encoding, sending emails, or generating reports can be pushed into a Redis-backed queue. Separate worker processes later consume those jobs asynchronously. This helps applications remain responsive even under heavy load.

of distributed systems: rate limiting, distributed locks, counters, leaderboards, live analytics, websocket coordination, and real-time notifications. Its sorted sets, in particular, became famous because they efficiently support ranking systems and priority queues.
